common_name: Akebono Cast Iron Plant (Frosted-New-Growth Deep-Shade Aspidistra)

planting.note: Divide and transplant clumps into humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade during mild spring weather, keeping newly split rhizomes evenly moist until re-established.

directions: Akebono is a cast iron plant selection grown for its new leaves, which emerge heavily flushed with creamy white to soft pink before gradually greening with age, giving each clump a shifting two-tone look through the growing season. Like the species, it tolerates deep shade, dry spells, and root competition from nearby trees once established, making it useful where few other foliage plants will grow. Keep it out of direct sun, which can scorch the pale new growth, and provide steady but infrequent watering rather than consistently damp soil. Divide congested clumps in spring if you want to increase your stock or renew an overcrowded planting.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Nina Cast Iron Plant (Compact White-Margined Dwarf Aspidistra)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to deep shade, choosing a sheltered spot since this dwarf selection is slower to recover from cold damage than larger cast iron plants.

directions: Nina is a compact, dwarf cast iron plant selection with narrow, dark green leaves edged in a crisp creamy-white margin, reaching only a fraction of the height of the straight species. Its smaller stature makes it well suited to tight shaded beds, woodland path edges, or containers where a full-size Aspidistra elatior would quickly outgrow the space. It shares the genus's tolerance for deep shade, irregular watering, and poor soil once established, asking for little beyond protection from hard freezes and direct midday sun. Divide slow-spreading clumps in spring only when you want additional plants, since established groupings resent frequent disturbance.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Oblanceolate-Leaf Cast Iron Plant (Broad-Bladed Chinese Aspidistra)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring and transplant into humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade, firming soil around roots and watering well until new growth appears.

directions: Aspidistra oblanceifolia is a clump-forming Chinese species named for its broad, oblanceolate leaves, which taper gradually toward the base on fairly long petioles and form a dense, arching rosette. Its low-growing, slow-spreading habit and tolerance of deep shade make it a useful groundcover beneath trees and shrubs where turf and most flowering perennials fail. Like other Aspidistra species it produces small, urn-shaped flowers near the soil surface, usually unnoticed unless leaf litter is cleared away from the crown. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil with steady but infrequent moisture, and divide congested clumps in spring to propagate or control spread.

common_name: Tailed-Flower Cast Iron Plant (Fine-Leaved Chinese Aspidistra)

planting.note: Divide and transplant rhizomes in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade, keeping the planting evenly moist until it re-establishes.

directions: Aspidistra caudata is a Chinese woodland species with slender, arching, lance-shaped leaves that give established clumps a finer, more graceful texture than the broad-leaved cast iron plant of typical gardens. Its epithet refers to the elongated, tail-like appendages on its small ground-level flowers, a feature shared with several of its Chinese relatives and more easily seen after clearing fallen leaves from the crown. It accepts deep, dry shade and root competition from established trees once settled in, asking only for humus-rich, well-drained soil and occasional watering during extended drought. Propagate by dividing rhizomes in spring, since it spreads slowly from the clump margin.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
